title: What is autoboxing and unboxing, what performance problem does autoboxing cause in loops, and how does the Integer cache (-128..127) affect `==`?
shortTitle: What is autoboxing, unboxing, and the Integer cache?

s1_definition.profdef: Autoboxing is the automatic conversion the compiler inserts from a primitive to its wrapper object, for example turning an int into an Integer when an Integer is expected, and unboxing is the reverse conversion from a wrapper back to its primitive. The compiler implements autoboxing by calling the wrapper's static valueOf method and unboxing by calling the wrapper's xxxValue method. Because autoboxing allocates a wrapper object on the heap, doing it repeatedly inside a loop creates many short-lived objects and significant garbage collection pressure, which is a real performance problem. Additionally, Integer.valueOf returns cached, shared instances for the range minus one hundred twenty eight to one hundred twenty seven, so two autoboxed Integers in that range are the same object and compare equal with the reference operator, while outside that range they are distinct objects and compare unequal, which is why reference comparison on wrappers is unreliable.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a primitive is like a bare number scribbled on a slip, and a wrapper object is like that same number placed inside an official sealed envelope with a tracking label. Autoboxing is the clerk automatically sealing a bare number into an envelope whenever the system demands an envelope, and unboxing is tearing the envelope open to read the bare number again. Sealing envelopes is cheap once, but doing it a million times in a loop means printing a million envelopes, which clogs the mail room, which is the garbage collection pressure. The cache is a tray of pre-printed envelopes for small common amounts from minus one hundred twenty eight to one hundred twenty seven, so when two small amounts are requested they hand out the very same pre-printed envelope, meaning the two references point to one object. For larger amounts they print fresh envelopes each time, so the references differ even when the amounts match.
s1_definition.oneliner: Autoboxing wraps a primitive into an object via valueOf and unboxing extracts it via xxxValue; boxing in loops creates garbage, and because valueOf caches minus one hundred twenty eight to one hundred twenty seven, `==` on wrappers only accidentally works inside that range.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Autoboxing is the automatic conversion the compiler inserts from a primitive to its wrapper object, for example turning an int into an Integer when an Integer is expected, and unboxing is the reverse conversion from a wrapper back to its primitive. The compiler implements autoboxing by calling the wrapper's static valueOf method and unboxing by calling the wrapper's xxxValue method. Because autoboxing allocates a wrapper object on the heap, doing it repeatedly inside a loop creates many short-lived objects and significant garbage collection pressure, which is a real performance problem. Additionally, Integer.valueOf returns cached, shared instances for the range minus one hundred twenty eight to one hundred twenty seven, so two autoboxed Integers in that range are the same object and compare equal with the reference operator, while outside that range they are distinct objects and compare unequal, which is why reference comparison on wrappers is unreliable.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a primitive is like a bare number scribbled on a slip, and a wrapper object is like that same number placed inside an official sealed envelope with a tracking label. Autoboxing is the clerk automatically sealing a bare number into an envelope whenever the system demands an envelope, and unboxing is tearing the envelope open to read the bare number again. Sealing envelopes is cheap once, but doing it a million times in a loop means printing a million envelopes, which clogs the mail room, which is the garbage collection pressure. The cache is a tray of pre-printed envelopes for small common amounts from minus one hundred twenty eight to one hundred twenty seven, so when two small amounts are requested they hand out the very same pre-printed envelope, meaning the two references point to one object. For larger amounts they print fresh envelopes each time, so the references differ even when the amounts match.

**One line to remember:** Autoboxing wraps a primitive into an object via valueOf and unboxing extracts it via xxxValue; boxing in loops creates garbage, and because valueOf caches minus one hundred twenty eight to one hundred twenty seven, `==` on wrappers only accidentally works inside that range.

sections.s2_technical:
Autoboxing happens anywhere the compiler sees a primitive where a wrapper is expected. For example `Integer count = 5;` is compiled as `Integer count = Integer.valueOf(5);`. The same occurs when you put an int into a collection, since generics only hold objects, so `List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(); list.add(7);` boxes the seven. Unboxing happens where a primitive is expected but a wrapper is supplied, so `int c = count;` is compiled as `int c = count.intValue();`, and arithmetic like `count + 1` unboxes count to an int first.

The performance problem in loops comes from repeated allocation. Consider summing amounts with an accidental Integer accumulator: `Integer total = 0; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) total += amounts[i];`. Each iteration unboxes total to int, adds, then autoboxes the result back into a brand new Integer via valueOf, because total is an Integer. For a million iterations that is roughly a million wrapper allocations, all immediately garbage, which hammers the young generation and slows the loop dramatically compared with using a primitive long accumulator that allocates nothing.

The Integer cache is the second major effect. Integer.valueOf is specified to cache and reuse instances for all int values from minus one hundred twenty eight to one hundred twenty seven inclusive. So `Integer a = 100; Integer b = 100;` both receive the same cached object, and `a == b` is true because the references are identical. But `Integer a = 1000; Integer b = 1000;` each allocate a new Integer outside the cache, so `a == b` is false even though the numeric values match. This makes the reference equality operator unreliable for wrappers; the correct comparison is always `a.equals(b)` or unboxing to primitives, which compare by value.

Several senior nuances matter in banking code. First, the cache upper bound is tunable with the JVM flag java.lang.Integer.IntegerCache.high, so the exact boundary where == stops working can shift per deployment, which is another reason never to rely on it. Second, Long, Short, Byte, and Character also cache small values, while Float and Double never cache, so == on boxed floating wrappers is always a new object. Third, unboxing a null wrapper throws NullPointerException, so an Integer that is null being used in arithmetic or an if condition blows up, which is a frequent bug when wrappers come from maps or nullable database columns. The practical rules are to use primitives for arithmetic and loops, to use wrappers only when an object is genuinely required such as inside collections or for a nullable value, and to always compare wrappers with equals rather than the reference operator.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A batch job sums a million transaction amounts, and a developer accidentally declared the running total as an Integer instead of a primitive, and the job ran noticeably slower and churned the heap. This is exactly the autoboxing-in-a-loop allocation problem.

Problem 2 — A validation check compared two account risk codes using the reference equality operator, and it worked for small codes but silently failed for larger codes above one hundred twenty seven. This is exactly the Integer cache making == unreliable.

Problem 3 — A lookup of a customer's pending-transaction count returned a null Integer from a map, and using it in arithmetic threw a NullPointerException. This is exactly unboxing a null wrapper.

The code contains a `BoxingDemo` main class that times a boxed versus primitive summation loop, demonstrates == inside and outside the cache range, and shows a null-unboxing NullPointerException handled safely.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: five million iterations, two pairs of Integers (one pair inside the cache, one outside), and a map lookup that returns null.

Step 1 — The boxed loop starts with an Integer total of zero, which is really the cached Integer zero. Each iteration unboxes total to an int, adds one, and autoboxes the result back by calling Integer.valueOf, which for values above the cache allocates a new Integer object. Over five million iterations this creates roughly five million short-lived objects that become garbage immediately.

Step 2 — The primitive loop does the same arithmetic with a primitive long. No object is ever created; the value lives in a register or stack slot and is simply incremented, so it finishes far faster and allocates nothing.

Step 3 — The program prints the two elapsed times, and the boxed loop is dramatically slower because the garbage collector must repeatedly clean the young generation.

Step 4 — Two Integers holding one hundred are compared with the reference operator. Because one hundred is inside the cache range, Integer.valueOf returned the same shared object for both, so the references are identical and the comparison is true.

Step 5 — Two Integers holding one thousand are compared the same way. One thousand is outside the cache, so each was a fresh object, the references differ, and the comparison is false even though the values match. The equals comparison on the same pair is true because it compares values.

Step 6 — A map lookup for Priya's pending count returns null because the key is absent. Assigning that null Integer to an int triggers unboxing, which calls intValue on null and throws a NullPointerException, caught and logged with its stack trace. The safe version uses getOrDefault to supply zero.


sections.s5b_flow:
```
  int primitive  ───autobox (Integer.valueOf)───→  Integer object (heap)
  Integer object ───unbox   (intValue())      ───→  int primitive

  ── Loop cost ──
  Integer total = 0
    │ iteration i:
    ▼
  unbox total → int → +1 → Integer.valueOf(result) → NEW Integer (if > 127)
    │ ×5,000,000
    ▼
  ~5,000,000 garbage objects → GC pressure → SLOW (41 ms)

  long total = 0
    │ iteration i: total += 1  (register/stack, no object)
    ▼
  0 allocations → FAST (3 ms)

  ── Integer cache (-128..127) ──
  Integer.valueOf(100) ─┐
                        ├─→ SAME cached object → 100 == 100  TRUE
  Integer.valueOf(100) ─┘
  Integer.valueOf(1000) → NEW object ─┐
                                      ├─→ diff refs → 1000 == 1000 FALSE
  Integer.valueOf(1000) → NEW object ─┘
  always correct: a.equals(b) → value compare → TRUE

  ── Null unbox ──
  map.get("CUR3001") → null → int x = null → intValue() on null → NPE
  getOrDefault("CUR3001", 0) → 0 → safe
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Autoboxing is the automatic conversion the compiler inserts from a primitive to its wrapper object, and unboxing is the reverse. Under the hood, autoboxing calls the wrapper's valueOf method, so writing Integer count equals five actually compiles to Integer dot valueOf of five, and unboxing calls intValue, so using that Integer in arithmetic silently extracts the primitive first. This is convenient, but it hides real costs that matter in production banking code.

The performance problem shows up in loops. If I accidentally make a running total an Integer instead of a primitive, every iteration unboxes it, adds, and then boxes the result back into a brand new Integer object through valueOf. Over millions of transactions in a batch summation that is millions of short-lived objects, all immediately garbage, which pounds the young generation and slows the job. The fix is simply to accumulate in a primitive long or double, which allocates nothing. I have seen a batch aggregation run many times faster just by changing the accumulator type from a wrapper to a primitive.

The Integer cache is the second effect, and it is why reference equality on wrappers is unreliable. Integer dot valueOf caches and reuses the same object for all values from minus one hundred twenty eight to one hundred twenty seven. So two Integers holding one hundred are the same cached object and compare true with the reference operator, but two Integers holding one thousand are separate objects and compare false even though the values are identical. This means I must always compare wrappers with the equals method, which compares values, and never with the reference operator, which compares object identity.

The senior nuances I always add are three. First, that cache boundary is tunable with the JVM flag for the Integer cache high value, so the exact point where reference comparison appears to work can shift between deployments, which is one more reason never to depend on it. Second, Long, Short, Byte, and Character cache small values too, while Float and Double never cache. Third, and most dangerous in banking, unboxing a null wrapper throws a NullPointerException, so an Integer pulled from a map or a nullable database column that happens to be null will blow up the moment it is used in arithmetic or a condition. My rules are therefore firm: use primitives for arithmetic and loops, use wrappers only when an object is genuinely required such as inside a collection or for a nullable value, compare wrappers with equals, and guard against null before unboxing, often with getOrDefault.

---

keyPoints: Autoboxing: compiler converts int to Integer via Integer.valueOf()
Unboxing: compiler converts Integer to int via intValue()
Integer cache: -128 to 127 reuses same objects — == works in this range
Outside cache range, == compares references (fails), use .equals()
